article.contentMarkdown:
# Ganesh Chaturthi Board Decoration for a School or Office Notice Board

A Ganesh Chaturthi board decoration is not a small mandap. It is an A1 notice board — 594 × 841 mm of paper held up by pins — standing unattended in a corridor from Monday 14 September to Friday 25 September 2026.

Four constraints follow, and no home decoration guide states any of them: no flame, no water, ten days of shoulders brushing past, and a reader who is walking instead of sitting. SubhSandesh has measured 3,894 personalised pages created since 2026-03-12, across 15 page types, and 46,005 recorded views of shared pages — none of them on a notice board, because a corridor is the one surface a link cannot reach. This is a paper-and-pins problem, and those four constraints are the design brief.

## What an A1 notice board gives you to work with

An A1 sheet is 0.5 square metres. Allow a 30 mm pinning margin at every edge and you have roughly 0.45 m² of usable face — about two open newspapers side by side.

That is the reason the advice here runs opposite to every festive listicle: the question is not what else you can add, but what you are prepared to leave off.

## Constraint one: no flame and no water, because nobody is watching it

A diya, an agarbatti stand or a string of fairy lights with a trailing plug all assume somebody is in the room. A corridor board at 9 p.m. on a Thursday has nobody in the room, and the surface it is pinned to is cellulose.

The National Bureau of Standards ran twenty full-scale room-corner tests on eight interior finish materials for Technical Note 879 in 1975, and used the ignition of **newsprint** as one of its indicators for when a room's combustible contents become involved. It put 450 to 650 °C as the boundary between limited and full involvement. Paper is what goes first, and an A1 board is paper.

Water is the quieter failure. Fresh flowers need a reservoir, a reservoir on a vertical board leaks down the face, and wet chart paper gains weight and sags until the pin holes tear open. Dry marigold strings are fine; anything with a container behind it is not.

## Constraint two: ten days of shoulders brushing past

Pin the sheet at its four corners and it will be flapping by day three, because a corridor board gets brushed at shoulder height by everyone who passes. Pin every 100 mm along the top edge and every 150 mm down the sides instead, and put the pins through a folded 15 mm hem rather than a single thickness.

Anything with mass loses. Papier-mâché figures, clay Ganeshas and glued-on thermocol shapes all pull straight down on a paper sheet held by steel points, and they come off in the first week. Cut-paper and folded-paper elements weigh almost nothing and survive the full 14 to 25 September span.

No published research on pin retention in soft-board displays turned up, so treat the spacing above as workshop practice rather than a measured finding.

## Constraint three: the reader is walking, so you get about nine words

This is the constraint that decides the layout, and no page on this keyword mentions it. A corridor reader is moving, so the binding limit is not letter height — it is how many words fit inside the time the board is in view.

Banerjee, Maurya and Lämmel reviewed pedestrian flow studies across several countries for *Collective Dynamics* in 2018 and reported free-flow walking speeds on sidewalk facilities of 65 to 85 metres per minute, mean 79 m/min. That is about 1.3 metres per second.

Brysbaert's 2019 meta-analysis of 190 studies and 18,573 participants puts average adult silent reading for English non-fiction at 238 words per minute, and oral reading at 183 wpm. Multiply it out: a board legible over a three-metre approach is in useful view for roughly 2.3 seconds, which at 238 wpm is **about nine words**.

So the headline is nine words or fewer, and the rest is either decoration or content for the one person in twenty who stops. Letter height still matters — cap heights in the tens of millimetres, to be readable at three metres at all — but the word budget is what people get wrong.

## Constraint four: leave about a third of the board empty

Barrett, Davies, Zhang and Barrett assessed 153 classrooms in 27 schools against the academic progress of the 3,766 pupils in them, published in *Building and Environment* in 2015 under a CC BY licence. Seven design parameters together explained 16% of the variation in progress, and one of them, Complexity, measures how coherent or chaotic a room's visual display is.

What matters for a notice board is the shape of that relationship. Complexity turned out to be curvilinear: both high-Complexity and low-Complexity classrooms scored poorly, while intermediate values scored highly. Complexity and Colour together accounted for 23% of the modelled effect.

Hanley and colleagues took the same question to eye-tracking in *Developmental Psychology* 53(7):1265–1275 in 2017. Children scored worse on worksheets after lessons filmed against high visual display than after the same lessons with none, and display dwell time was the strongest predictor of how little they learned. Only the abstract is readable without a subscription, so that is all this post claims from it.

Read together: one focal Ganesha, a nine-word line and real empty margins beat a board covered edge to edge. Aim for about two-thirds coverage and stop.

## The one-hour build, from a stationery cupboard

Two students with chart paper, scissors, a glue stick and a marker set can finish this in an hour. In order of what to do first:

### 1. One Ganesha silhouette, cut once

Fold a sheet of dark chart paper in half, cut half a Ganesha profile, open it out. One symmetrical shape, roughly 400 mm tall, pinned centre-left. It reads at three metres because it is a silhouette, not a drawing.

### 2. The nine-word line, in 60 mm letters

Cut or print letters at about 60 mm cap height. "Happy Ganesh Chaturthi 2026" is four words and leaves five for the class, the department or a wish.

### 3. A folded-fan border instead of flowers

Concertina-fold strips of orange and yellow paper into fans and pin them along the top edge only. No water, no weight, and they hold shape for ten days.

### 4. A modak grid, not a modak pile

Six to nine paper modak from a single template, pinned in a grid with even gaps. The grid is what makes it read as pattern rather than clutter.

### 5. A printed link in the bottom corner

One line of 20 mm text with a short URL or a QR code — the only element anyone outside the corridor can act on.

## What each element costs, and what it reaches

| Element | Materials | Build time | Holds to 25 Sept | Reach beyond the corridor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ganesha silhouette | ₹20 chart paper | 15 min | Yes, if hemmed | None |
| Nine-word headline | ₹30 letters/print | 15 min | Yes | None |
| Folded-fan border | ₹25 craft paper | 15 min | Yes | None |
| Paper modak grid | ₹15 offcuts | 10 min | Yes | None |
| Printed link or QR | ₹5 print | 5 min | Yes | 11.8 average views per created page, 49.6% of them opened on a phone |

The last row is the only one with a number in the right-hand column, and that is the honest shape of this. Average views per created page is 11.8, and 49.6% of shared pages are opened on a phone — which is why a printed link works at all: whoever scans it is already holding the device that opens it.

## When boards like this actually get made

Nobody starts ten days early. SubhSandesh's own lead-time measurement is on **Raksha Bandhan 2026, not Ganesh Chaturthi** — a different festival, and a one-day one against Ganesh Chaturthi's ten — and **n = 89 pages is small**, so no per-template or per-region rate can be drawn from it. With those two caveats stated: 49.4% of those pages were built on the festival day itself, 27.0% the day before, and the median lead time was 0 days.

There is also no Ganesh Chaturthi page-creation data at all yet, because the [Ganesh Chaturthi page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-ganesh-chaturthi) went live on 2026-09-10, four days before the festival. Which is to say: plan the board for the hour you will actually have, not the weekend you imagine having.

## How anyone outside that corridor sees it

A notice board has exactly one audience: people who walk past it. Parents, alumni, the branch in another city and the grandparent who would have liked to see it all get nothing, and no amount of decoration fixes that.

A printed link or QR in the corner is the fix, and it costs five rupees. The [written build guide for the Ganesh Chaturthi page](https://subhsandesh.in/guides/happy-ganesh-chaturthi) covers what to have ready before you start.

## When a board is the wrong answer

If the audience is twelve people in one room, a board is over-built — put the effort into the room. If the corridor is a back stairwell nobody uses, the board is invisible whatever you pin to it.

And SubhSandesh is no use for the corridor itself. Occasion-dated pages, every festival plus every wedding type, are 144 of 3,894 pages, 3.7% — the platform is 96.3% romantic and everyday pages, it prints nothing, and it will not hold a pin.

## Watch the page get built

Ninety seconds, start to finish — the aarti going round, the five offerings, and the box at the end where they write a line back to you: [Ganesh Chaturthi Wishes Online — Full Walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mpWiv5T59QY). More page walkthroughs on Instagram: [@subhsandesh_official](https://www.instagram.com/subhsandesh_official).

## Sources

- Fang (1975), [*Fire Buildup in a Room and the Role of Interior Finish Materials*](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/TN/nbstechnicalnote879.pdf), NBS Technical Note 879.
- Banerjee, Maurya & Lämmel (2018), [pedestrian flow characteristics and level of service](https://collective-dynamics.eu/index.php/cod/article/view/A17), *Collective Dynamics* 3.
- Brysbaert (2019), [How many words do we read per minute?](https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/xynwg), PsyArXiv preprint.
- Barrett, Davies, Zhang & Barrett (2015), [classroom design and pupils' learning](https://eprints.hud.ac.uk/id/eprint/29830/1/1-s2.0-S0360132315000700-main.pdf), *Building and Environment* 89:118–133, CC BY.
- Hanley et al. (2017), [Classroom displays — attraction or distraction?](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/28471220), *Developmental Psychology* 53(7):1265–1275, abstract only.

failed.why: Four of the five sources are locked to this subject (classroom display density, corridor walking speed, interior-finish fire behaviour, an eye-tracking study of wall displays). Brysbaert's reading-rate meta-analysis is not: 238 wpm could sit unchanged in this batch's ganesh-chaturthi-calligraphy or ganesh-chaturthi-logo-design posts. It is retained because the nine-word budget cannot be derived without a reading rate, but it does not cleanly pass the test and is recorded as a failure rather than argued away.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine would cite this for one thing the three live decoration siblings and the whole SERP lack: a stated word budget for a reader who is walking - about nine words, from 65-85 m/min free-flow walking speeds against a 238 wpm silent reading rate - plus the classroom-display finding that display Complexity is curvilinear, so two-thirds coverage beats edge-to-edge. Seven of the ten results on this keyword are Pinterest or YouTube and the single prose incumbent cites nothing, so there is no research-backed page to displace; the flip side is that image feeds are hard to outrank on an image-intent keyword no matter how good the prose is, and subhsandesh.in has no authority in the school-craft space. TOOL LIMITATION, recorded per BRIEF 4: the WebSearch tool is US-locale only - there is no gl=in - so every SERP behind the cannibalisation gate is a US capture and the real India SERP may differ. The session also exhausted its WebSearch budget (200/200) after three of four planned captures, so the third sibling's top 10 is taken from that sibling's own one-day-old research brief rather than re-run; the intersection there is 0 against a threshold of 3, so the verdict holds, but the capture is second-hand. The weakest part of the post is constraint two: the pin spacing is craft practice with no citable study behind it, and it is recorded as an audit failure rather than dressed up.
